title: Cell - The Unit of Life
description: Grade 11 Biology: cell theory, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells, the plasma membrane and cell wall, the endomembrane system, mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes and the nucleus.

topics.title: Cell Theory; Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
topics.concept:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms — the smallest unit capable of independent existence. It was first seen by Robert Hooke (1665, in cork) and the living cell by Leeuwenhoek.

The cell theory, given by Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) and extended by Rudolf Virchow, states that: (1) all living organisms are made of cells and their products; (2) the cell is the basic unit of life; and (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).

Cells are of two fundamental types:

  • Prokaryotic cells — found in bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma. They are smaller and simpler, with no true (membrane-bound) nucleus (the genetic material lies free in a region called the nucleoid) and no membrane-bound organelles. They have a cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm with 70S ribosomes, and may have extra DNA called plasmids and a glycocalyx, flagella and pili.
  • Eukaryotic cells — found in protists, plants, fungi and animals. They are larger and complex, with a true nucleus bounded by a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, etc.) and 80S ribosomes.

Plant cells differ from animal cells in having a cell wall, large central vacuoles and plastids (e.g. chloroplasts); animal cells lack these but have a centrosome and small vacuoles.

examples.problem: Example 1: State the cell theory and name the scientist who added that cells arise from pre-existing cells.
examples.solution:
Recall the cell theory and its contributors.

  • Cell theory: all organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; all cells come from pre-existing cells.
  • Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
examples.answer: Cell theory: organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells (added by Rudolf Virchow).

examples.problem: Example 2: Give two key differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
examples.solution:
Compare the nucleus and organelles.

  • Prokaryotes lack a true (membrane-bound) nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • Eukaryotes have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
examples.answer: Prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while eukaryotes have both.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name two structures present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell.
examples.solution:
Plant cells have certain extra structures.

  • Cell wall.
  • Plastids (e.g. chloroplasts) and a large central vacuole.
examples.answer: A cell wall and plastids (chloroplasts) — and a large central vacuole — are present in plant cells but absent in animal cells.

recap:
• The cell is the basic unit of life; first seen by Hooke.
  • Cell theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow): organisms are made of cells; cells are the basic unit; cells arise from pre-existing cells.
  • Prokaryotes = no true nucleus / no membrane-bound organelles (70S ribosomes); eukaryotes = true nucleus + organelles (80S).
  • Plant cells uniquely have a cell wall, plastids, large vacuole.

quiz.q: Cells that lack a true (membrane-bound) nucleus are:
quiz.explanation: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus; the DNA lies in a nucleoid.

quiz.q: The statement that all cells arise from pre-existing cells was given by:
quiz.explanation: Rudolf Virchow added that new cells come from pre-existing cells.

topics.title: The Cell Membrane, Cell Wall and Endomembrane System
topics.concept:
The plasma membrane is the outer boundary of the cell. It is made mainly of lipids (a phospholipid bilayer) and proteins. The accepted fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson) describes it as a fluid lipid bilayer in which proteins float like a mosaic. The membrane is selectively permeable, controlling what enters and leaves: by passive transport (diffusion, osmosis — no energy) and active transport (against the gradient, using ATP).

The cell wall is a non-living, rigid outer covering present in plant cells, fungi and bacteria. In plants it is made of cellulose; it gives shape, support and protection, and prevents the cell from bursting.

Several membrane-bound organelles work together as the endomembrane system:

  • Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) — a network of tubules: rough ER (bears ribosomes; makes proteins) and smooth ER (no ribosomes; makes lipids).
  • Golgi apparatus — stacked flattened sacs that modify, pack and dispatch materials (the cell's 'post office'); also forms lysosomes.
  • Lysosomes — membrane sacs full of digestive enzymes; they digest worn-out parts and foreign material (the 'suicide bags' of the cell).
  • Vacuoles — membrane-bound spaces for storage of water, food and wastes; large and central in plant cells (bounded by the tonoplast).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the model that explains the structure of the plasma membrane and state its main idea.
examples.solution:
The membrane is described by a particular model.

  • The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson).
  • It describes a fluid lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it like a mosaic.
examples.answer: The fluid mosaic model — a fluid lipid bilayer with proteins embedded/floating in it like a mosaic.

examples.problem: Example 2: Differentiate rough ER and smooth ER.
examples.solution:
The two types of ER differ in ribosomes and function.

  • Rough ER bears ribosomes and synthesises proteins.
  • Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids.
examples.answer: Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER has no ribosomes and makes lipids.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are lysosomes called the 'suicide bags' of the cell?
examples.solution:
Lysosomes contain powerful enzymes.

  • They are filled with digestive enzymes.
  • If they burst, the enzymes can digest the cell's own contents, causing its death.
examples.answer: Because they contain digestive enzymes that, if released, can digest and destroy the cell itself.

recap:
• Plasma membrane = phospholipid bilayer + proteins (fluid mosaic model); selectively permeable.
  • Cell wall (cellulose in plants) gives shape, support and protection.
  • Endomembrane system: ER (rough = protein, smooth = lipid), Golgi (modify/pack/dispatch), lysosomes ('suicide bags'), vacuoles (storage).

quiz.q: The structure of the plasma membrane is best explained by the:
quiz.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a fluid lipid bilayer with proteins.

quiz.q: Which organelle modifies, packs and dispatches materials in the cell?
quiz.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials.

topics.title: Energy Organelles, the Cytoskeleton and the Nucleus
topics.concept:
Some organelles produce energy or organise the cell:

  • Mitochondria — the 'powerhouses of the cell'; double-membraned, with the inner membrane folded into cristae. They carry out aerobic respiration to produce ATP. They have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes (semi-autonomous).
  • Plastids (in plant cells) — chloroplasts (green, contain chlorophyll, site of photosynthesis; have stacks of thylakoids called grana in a stroma), chromoplasts (coloured, give colour to flowers/fruits) and leucoplasts (colourless, store food). Chloroplasts too have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
  • Ribosomes — non-membrane organelles made of RNA and protein; the site of protein synthesis (70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes).
  • Centrosome (in animal cells) — contains two centrioles; helps form the spindle during cell division.
  • Cytoskeleton — a network of protein filaments (microtubules, microfilaments) giving shape, support and helping movement.

The nucleus is the control centre of the cell. It is bounded by a double nuclear membrane with pores, and contains a jelly-like nucleoplasm, one or more nucleoli (make ribosomes), and the genetic material as chromatin. During cell division the chromatin condenses into rod-like chromosomes, which carry the genes (DNA) responsible for heredity. The nucleus controls all cell activities and inheritance.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why are mitochondria called the 'powerhouses of the cell'?
examples.solution:
Mitochondria release energy.

  • They carry out aerobic respiration.
  • This releases energy stored as ATP for the cell's use.
examples.answer: Because they carry out aerobic respiration and produce ATP, the energy currency of the cell.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the three types of plastids and the function of each.
examples.solution:
Plastids are of three kinds.

  • Chloroplasts — photosynthesis (green).
  • Chromoplasts — give colour to flowers and fruits.
  • Leucoplasts — store food (colourless).
examples.answer: Chloroplasts (photosynthesis), chromoplasts (colour to flowers/fruits) and leucoplasts (food storage).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the role of the nucleus, and what does the chromatin become during cell division?
examples.solution:
The nucleus is the control centre.

  • It controls all the activities of the cell and carries the hereditary material.
  • During division, the chromatin condenses into chromosomes.
examples.answer: The nucleus controls cell activities and inheritance; during division the chromatin condenses into chromosomes.

recap:
• Mitochondria = powerhouses (aerobic respiration → ATP; cristae; own DNA).
  • Plastids: chloroplasts (photosynthesis), chromoplasts (colour), leucoplasts (storage).
  • Ribosomes = protein synthesis; centrosome = spindle (animal); cytoskeleton = shape/support.
  • Nucleus = control centre; contains nucleolus and chromatin → chromosomes (carry genes/DNA).

quiz.q: The site of protein synthesis in a cell is the:
quiz.explanation: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

quiz.q: Photosynthesis takes place in which plastid?
quiz.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

questions.q: The basic structural and functional unit of life is the:
questions.explanation: The cell is the basic unit of life.

questions.q: The cell was first observed (in cork) by:
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke first observed cells in cork (1665).

questions.q: 'All cells arise from pre-existing cells' was stated by:
questions.explanation: Virchow extended the cell theory with this statement.

questions.q: Prokaryotic cells lack:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no true nucleus; DNA lies in a nucleoid.

questions.q: Which structure is present in a plant cell but NOT an animal cell?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cell wall (also plastids, large vacuole); animal cells do not.

questions.q: The plasma membrane is best described by the:
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane structure.

questions.q: The plant cell wall is mainly made of:
questions.explanation: The plant cell wall is made of cellulose.

questions.q: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is the site of synthesis of:
questions.explanation: Rough ER bears ribosomes and synthesises proteins.

questions.q: The organelle that modifies, packs and dispatches cell products is the:
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials.

questions.q: Lysosomes are called the 'suicide bags' because they contain:
questions.explanation: Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes that can destroy the cell.

questions.q: The 'powerhouse of the cell', producing ATP, is the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to make ATP.

questions.q: Photosynthesis occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

questions.q: Ribosomes are the site of:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes synthesise proteins.

questions.q: The control centre of the cell is the:
questions.explanation: The nucleus controls all cell activities and inheritance.

questions.q: During cell division, chromatin condenses to form:
questions.explanation: Chromatin condenses into rod-like chromosomes during division.

questions.q: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes. This supports the idea that they:
questions.explanation: Their own DNA and 70S ribosomes suggest an endosymbiotic prokaryotic origin.

questions.q: A cell actively pumps ions in against their concentration gradient. This requires:
questions.explanation: Moving substances against the gradient is active transport, which uses ATP.

questions.q: A gland cell that secretes large amounts of protein would be expected to have abundant:
questions.explanation: Protein synthesis and packaging need plenty of rough ER and Golgi.

questions.q: Why can a plant cell placed in pure water not burst, while an animal cell may?
options: The rigid cellulose cell wall resists the swelling
Animal cells have a cell wall
questions.explanation: The plant cell wall withstands the turgor pressure, preventing bursting.

questions.q: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into cristae mainly to:
options: Increase the surface area for ATP-producing reactions
questions.explanation: Cristae increase surface area for the enzymes of respiration, boosting ATP output.

questions.q: Red blood cells of mammals lack a nucleus, which means they cannot:
options: Divide or make new proteins, so they have a short lifespan
questions.explanation: Without a nucleus they cannot divide or synthesise proteins, limiting their lifespan.
